The sky as telescopes see it

Clouds and galaxies drawn in 3D from photographs. Leaving goes back to Earth.

Open the trip: The sky as telescopes see it

With your own eyes

This is the Orion Nebula roughly as your eye would see it at a telescope: a faint grey glow. The gas is real, but it is faint, and in the dark the eye sees no colour. It cannot save up light the way a camera can.

With a camera

A camera can keep its shutter open and let the light pile up. Now the colour is there. It was always there. The red is hydrogen gas. Its light here comes from a photograph taken through colour filters with an extra one for glowing hydrogen, so the red is stronger than an eye would find it.

A long exposure

Stretch a long exposure further and the faintest outer parts appear. Each cloud and galaxy on this trip is drawn in three dimensions, built from measurements of its shape, its light taken from telescope photographs. Its card lets you compare it with the photograph itself.

The Horsehead

Just beside Orion's belt, a dark cloud of dust stands in front of glowing gas, in the shape of a horse's head. Here the colours are chosen. The photograph it is built from took the light of single gases through narrow filters, and each gas was given a colour so the eye can tell them apart.

The Carina Nebula

A great cloud in the southern sky, in the constellation of the Keel. Monster stars live inside it. Their fierce winds and ultraviolet light are carving the gas into the shapes you see: walls, pillars and hollows, lit from within.

What Webb saw in the Tarantula

Seen from our side, this cloud's light is the Webb telescope's own picture. It is made in infrared light, which no eye can see, so every colour in it is chosen. Infrared passes through dust, and here it shows tens of thousands of young stars that no telescope had seen. The region is 340 light-years across, in a small galaxy beside ours.

The Trifid, from the newest telescope

The Trifid Nebula, with the dark lanes of dust that give it its name. It was among the very first pictures from the Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile, released in June 2025. For ten years that telescope will photograph the southern sky every few nights.

Another galaxy

Now far beyond our own galaxy. The Whirlpool is a spiral galaxy tens of millions of light-years away, seen face on. A smaller galaxy is passing behind it and tugging on one arm. The pink knots along the arms are clouds of hydrogen where new stars are forming.

A galaxy you can see for yourself

Andromeda, the nearest large galaxy to our own, two and a half million light-years off. You can see it without any telescope, as a faint smudge. How well you see it, like everything on this trip, depends on how dark your sky is.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, OpenNGC and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
